Nvidia’s Relief Rally Stalls
 
Plus, Anthropic dips below its IPO price, and the investors who won—and lost—in the Nvidia saga
 
By Heard on the Street Staff
 
 
CHIANG YING-YING/ASSOCIATED PRESS
 

This is an edition of the Markets P.M. newsletter, a recap of the day’s most important markets moves, delivered after the closing bell. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

What Happened in Markets Today

 

Nvidia dropped. Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia’s chief executive was welcomed Monday with a more than 31% surge in the AI chip giant’s stock. With the many challenges and threats still facing Nvidia and the whole AI ecosystem, though, the shine came off a bit on Tuesday. Nvidia’s shares ended down 5.9%—leaving them more than 10% lower than before Huang resigned earlier this month.

 

Anthropic fell. Last week’s surge of excitement about the AI lab’s IPO is proving short-lived. The company’s stock fell 6.5% to $81.90, below its $83 per share offering price.

 

A broader reversal for tech stocks took hold. Monday’s Huang-driven burst of excitement gave way to a down day for many tech names. CoreWeave, a cloud-computing company that Nvidia has a stake in, dropped nearly 12%. Analog Devices, a chip maker whose quarterly results Tuesday included a disappointing profit outlook, fell 17%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index fell 1.5%.

 

Other indexes were mixed. The S&P 500 fell 0.5%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 0.9%.

One Big Story

 
 
Lauren Cassidy, an Nvidia investor and chief investment officer at Founder ETFs. LAUREN CASSIDY
 

Many individual investors abandoned Nvidia when Huang resigned, convinced that the company had lost its verve without him. Then came Monday’s shocking news that Huang was back, sending its stock soaring and setting off a scramble to buy back into the company’s shares. Much money has been lost and gained in the tumult, including short sellers who made around $13.7 billion betting against the stock in the past week—only to lose about 90% of that amount after Monday’s rise.

• October personal-consumption expenditures data—which includes the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge—are due in the morning.

 

• New home sales data for October are also set for release.
